speechtext:
Hon. BROOKE CLAXTON (Minister of National Health and Welfare) moved the second reading of bill No. 252, to amend the Food and Drugs Act.
' Mr. G. RUSSELL BOUCHER (Carleton): Mr. Speaker, I do not like to delay the house at this late stage to talk about something that is diseased or putrid or rotten, but those words are within the nomenclature of the bill.
I am rising to question the competency of the federal parliament to pass this bill. We all know that under section 91 of the British North America Act certain powers are given to the dominion parliament to deal specifically with matters apart from those given to the provinces under section 92. This bill, from the very best of motives, may seek to make a meritorious change in the existing law, but before making this amendment, which does go a long way, we should see whether this parliament has power to give effect to it. I have had the opportunity of referring to a number of decisions, and I think before we pass this bill we should have an opinion from the Department of Justice on the question of jurisdiction that it involves.
Briefly it appears to me that the only way in which the dominion parliament can have competence in a matter of this kind having to do with civil rights is by saying that this is not one of the specific powers delegated to the provinces by section 92 but is a specific power given by section 91 to the dominion parliament or a general power not given to the provinces by section 92.
In the case of Toronto Electric Commission v. Snider, 1925, 2 D.L.R. page 16, their lordships held that in approaching problems of jurisdiction in matters of this kind we should ask ourselves:	(1) does the subject matter
fall within section 92; and (2) does the subject matter fall within section 91 of the
British North America Act? If it falls within neither of the enumerated heads, then the dominion has power under the general wording of section 91.
In the case of the Attorney General for Canada v. the Attorney General for Alberta, their lordships gave this decision:
It is their lordships' opinion, now clear, that excepting so far as the power can be involved in aid of capacity conferred independently under other words of section 91, the power to regulate trade and commerce cannot be relied upon as enabling the dominion parliament to regulate civil rights in the provinces.
, The same decision has been given in a number of other cases decided not only by the courts of Canada but in some cases by the privy council, and I mention specifically the famous Wharton case, 1914, 18 D.L.R., page 335; Rex v. Collins, 1926, 4 D.L.R., page 548, and King v. Eastern Terminal Elevator Company, 1925, 5 D.L.R., page 1. In these cases questions of this kind came specifically before the court, and it was held that as civil rights were specifically assigned to the provinces to deal with, the power of sale falls within that zone.
This bill seems to say that no one can sell or offer for sale certain commodities. It goes further than that and restricts it to food or drugs. In order to make this act effective I think the question of jurisdiction should be examined very carefully. In my opinion provincial enactments are necessary to give validity to legislation of this kind. By the act very wide power is given to the dominion to interfere with the sale of what are called drugs, and perhaps appliances, foods or materials. The meaning of "drugs" under this amendment will be greatly extended. Explanatory note 1 says:
It is therefore considered desirable that such authority be given in the interest of the public. Any regulations made under this authority will, for the most part, deal with newly-discovered drugs.
That protection may be required, but I see nothing in the bill to restrict its operation to newly discovered drugs. It goes much beyond that. I would therefore ask the minister to indicate at least the scope of the amended act and the opinion of the Department of Justice as to the competency of this parliament to pass such an act, and state whether or not to infringe upon the rights of the provinces given under the British North America Act. We should be very careful about questions of jurisdiction.

speakeroldname: Hon. BROOKE CLAXTON (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: LIMITATIONS UPON IMPORTATION AND SALE TO GENERAL PUBLIC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
this bill, which comes to us from the senate, has four sections. It makes what are intended
Food and Drugs Act

to be technical and non-controversial amendments in the Food and Drugs Act so as to permit of its being administered and applied to the greater advantage of the people of Canada. The remarks of the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Boucher) relate I think exclusively to the provisions of section 1 of the bill, under which the governor in council may have the power to pass regulations "defining the conditions of sale of any drug". The Department of Justice has been asked for an opinion on the validity of this legislation and has expressed the view that it is constitutional.
The Food and1 Drugs Act has a long ancestry. It dates back to the Adulteration Act of 1875, which was incorporated in the new Food and Drugs Act of 1920. The validity of the act and of the regulations passed under it was only challenged in one case as far as I know, that of Standard Sausage Company v. Lee, in which the British Columbia court of appeal unanimously affirmed the validity of the legislation.
The position taken by the hon. member for Carleton is, I understand, based on the proposed "defining the conditions of sale of any drug" being too wide and unrestricted. If those words were taken without reference to the general scope of the act it might well be feared that the federal government would seek to regulate conditions of sale of drugs in a way which related to property and civil rights and not to any of the powers of the federal government. We have considered that, and while it is never the intention to do anything beyond the general scope of this act or of the federal government-that of course is unquestioned-we have thought that in consequence of representations made on behalf of the pharmaceutical druggists of Canada it might be a good thing to limit this power, since it probably goes beyond anything which we might ever expect to exercise. In consequence I propose, when we reach the committee stage, to ask one of my colleagues to add at the end of paragraph (kk) the words "in the interest and for the protection of the public health", so as to make it quite clear that this additional power to make regulations would be definitely limited to the general scope of the act; that is, to regulations defining the conditions of sale of any drugs in the interest and for the protection of the public health". In other words the Department of National Health and Welfare, as part of the duty conferred upon it by this measure, seeks to carry out the provisions of the act in the interest of the health and welfare of the people of Canada but not from the point of view of any commercial interest.

Whether or not that could be done by the federal government does not enter into consideration here; that is not the intention; and in order to show more clearly what is the intention than was done in the bill which was put before the house I propose to ask a colleague when we reach the committee stage to move the amendment I have just read to the house.
I may say also that after the representations wTere made by representatives of the pharmaceutical trade we had a discussion with them, and I communicated the text of this amendment to them and they felt that that would take care of the situation.

subtopic: LIMITATIONS UPON IMPORTATION AND SALE TO GENERAL PUBLIC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a very important bill, and I suggest to the minister that there are three or four matters he might consider in relation to it. We have a committee of this house known as the committee on pensions and health. How does it come about that, on the eighty-fourth day of this session, this bill has not been before that committee? When the bill was introduced in another place there was a two-line debate; it went to a committee on second reading without any debate, nor was there any debate on third reading; then it came here.
Aou know, Mr. Speaker, that after every great war there is a deluge of medicines advertised on the market. The principles of this bill are contained in two sentences of the explanatory notes, which begin:
This1 is to permit of regulations being made for the protection of the pubic respecting the sale of any drug.
Nowadays most of the city papers are filled with advertisements of drugs, patent medicines, salves, and so on, any one of which is supposed to be a cure for ten or fifteen different diseases which have baffled the medical profession for many years. You can walk into a grocery store and buy them; you can buy them in departmental stores and elsewhere.
In 1927 the general Food and Drugs Act now to be amended evidently contained sufficient protection for the public, but, to quote the notes:
The present act limits such power-
That is, to sell drugs.
->to a substance which may be injurious to health.	.
One of the clauses refers to a commodity which contains rotten or diseased animal or vegetable substance. The hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) complained for years about drugs in liquid form-gin-which contain injurious ingredients, and on one occasion, discussing the matter with the then
JULY 19, i946
Food and Drugs Act
minister of health (Mr. Mackenzie) as an amateur to an expert he said he had had a chemical analysis made and it was not Holland gin and not gin at all.
Since the close of the war the act as it stands does not provide sufficient protection-

inasmuch as new drugs are being discovered which, until their full effect is known over a period of time, may . . . prove to be injurious to health.
Now. you have to read, with the sections of the act which the minister is amending, the regulations of the wartime prices and trade board. They passed absurd regulations which every drug store is compelled to carry out. What are those regulations? Well, if a medical doctor gives a man, be he rich or poor, a prescription, it can be filled only once; he has to go back to the medical man to get another order before the druggist will fill it. Sometimes these stores are closed at the week-end, and it reacts to the inconvenience of the public, particularly to people of the poorer classes in the cities and towns when a drug store is closed.
I cannot understand the present health act procedure. We have a committee on health; let us have a real committee on health, and do something, not come down to the house on the eighty-fourth day of the session saying: *"Here is a bill; pass it." This bill should have been properly considered by our health committee. May I ask the minister whether the representatives of the drug interests or of the college of pharmacy were before the committee in the other place?-because certainly they have had no opportunity to examine this bill.
Mind1 you, I am not opposing the bill. I believe the restrictions to-day are not what they should be. Drugs are being sold as such which are not drugs at all. Various mixtures and chemical compounds have been prepared and advertised in the newspapers, in three or four-line advertisements, "Communicate by letter or telephone with so and so, who has got a cure." We need an act which is a real health act to protect the public from all this quackery.
Not only that; a lot of things have been placed on the market which are poisoning the people-all kinds of moonshine. From health officers and from the college of physicians and others complaints have come about the loose way in which this particular problem is being handled. The time has come for a drastic national health reform, so that the consumer public will be protected, so that the people will know what are proper or at least noninjurious remedies. Some companies in the olden days used to get out almanacs at Christmas time of drugs which were a cure for
everything. If the Food and Drugs Act is to be properly administered there should be an attempt to deal with some of the offenders, and have an examination of some of the awful stuff people take which one hears about in the magistrates' and coroners' courts. The public are complaining about the different poisons which are put out-"hair tonics" and all that sort of thing; you can buy them right on the market. What is the department doing about it? The Department of Justice will not do anything. They refer complaints to the attorneys general of the provinces, and all they do is to refer it to the city and town and county police.
We need a reformation regarding the use of some of these drugs, the things which some poor people are drinking all day long, poisoning themselves. In fact many small children have been poisoned, because when the mothers and fathers are out some of them go to the cupboard and take a pill or something else of this kind.
Not only that, but I wish to say that if we are to have a department let us have a real one, not one which can do nothing more than say, on the eighty-fourth day of the session, "Pass this bill or leave it." Mind you, I believe the department may do quite a lot in protecting the consumer public. But there is no doubt that we should start on legislation like this early in the session. There are other measures which were placed on the order paper only yesterday. There are a large number of bills as to which we should have the opportunity of consulting professional men, legal men, physicians, dentists, veterinarians, and the college of pharmacy, but there is no opportunity of doing so here in the middle of July, when everybody is away.
So far as the principle of the bill is concerned I support it. Something must be done to curb the sale of the poisons which are now being sold, without proper control-I will not say in the drug stores, because the proprietors are good professional men who alike in peace and war have done laborious and efficient work-I do not know what we would have done without them-but considerable sales are made in some small corner general stores. Most of these remedies advertise in the papers, and you can get a bottle or two almost for the asking-three bottles for 50 cents while one bottle is "worth" 35 cents.
As I have said, the hon. member for Temis-couata started this discussion the year before last, to bring the Food and Drugs Act up to date, but nothing has been done to protect the public. I do hope we shall have drastic reform in this particular branch of health protection, so that the consumer public will be protected,
Food and Drugs Act

while legitimate drug stores are free dfrom some of Donald Gordon's regulations. One is that a physician cannot fill a prescription available for more than one order; he has to write a new prescription. I tell you, the public are sick and tired of that kind of bureaucracy, a year after the war has ended.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: LIMITATIONS UPON IMPORTATION AND SALE TO GENERAL PUBLIC
speechtext:
The main purpose that we have immediately in mind in this section is to regulate the sale of penicillin. That is already done in the United States and in the United Kingdom. The reason for seeking that power is that we have not the power under existing legislation and it is considered desirable by a large proportion of the medical profession, as well as by representatives of the provinces and officers of the department, that for some time at least penicillin should be sold only on a doctor's prescription.
Penicillin, so far as we know, is not injurious in itself, but it can be used in a way which may be injurious to the user if not used under a doctor's control. The reason is this: It is a very powerful drug; it is popularly described as a miracle worker, as indeed it is, when properly used. But some people have the idea that if they go to a druggist and buy some penicillin they are almost certain to be cured of any one of a number of diseases, including particularly gonorrhea and syphilis. Penicillin, used in the right doses and in the right way and at the right time, is a cure for gonorrhea and has a powerful effect on syphilis; but used in the wrong doses or in the wrong way or at the wrong time, it not only does not cure the disease but may itself set up immunity against the proper used of penicillin. In other words, the improper use of penicillin may not only fail to effect a cure but may prevent the proper use of the drug as a means of effecting the cure.
There are a number of drugs that work in that way and penicillin is said to be one of them. Further, the use of penicillin without proper advice may lead to certain germs of infection being killed by bringing into operation others which have been kept under control by the germs which are killed off. That has been pointed out in medical journals and in medical experience, and for these reasons we believe it is necessary for the time being at least to regulate penicillin and require that it be sold under doctor's prescription.
It is not the policy of the act to name single drugs, and we have not named penicillin or limited this power to pencillin because of the
LMr. Church.]
fact that exactly the same considerations apply to some of the other new drugs and also to streptomycin, and other drugs that may be brought into use from day to day, since the development of these new drugs is exceedingly rapid.
For that reason we have sought this power, which is along the lines of similar powers exercised in the United States and the United Kingdom. However, in order to limit it in accordance with the suggestion of the representatives of the trade, I am going to ask. my colleague the Secretary of State to move an amendment to section 1 of the bill.

subtopic: LIMITATIONS UPON IMPORTATION AND SALE TO GENERAL PUBLIC
speechtext: What control does the government exercise over the manufacture and distribution of penicillin? I am in agreement with giving the government control of these new drugs. It is essential, and the minister is quite right that the unguided use of penicillin may lead to some other difficulties after the drug has been used. People may use it to heal a cut or a wound or to get rid of a sore and then find that a disagreeable rash develops. I have knowledge of at least two instances in which this has happened. A physician has prescribed penicillin for the healing of a sore or for some other trouble of the kind, and afterwards there has developed a serious rash. I agree that the drug should be controlled. Many drugs are very simple things. They do not entail a great deal of expense in the manufacture and yet when people have to get them on a doctor's prescription they often find that apart from the cost of the prescription-no one objects to that, because the doctor usually does more than write a prescription-they are very expensive. Sometimes these things are patented; I do not know whether penicillin is patented or not. I see the minister shakes his head; I am glad to learn that it is not. What control is exercised in the manufacture and the distribution in order that the public may not be victimized by the price charged for this efficient drug?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: LIMITATIONS UPON IMPORTATION AND SALE TO GENERAL PUBLIC
speechtext:
The question of price
does not come under the control of this department, but under the wartime prices and trade board which has exercised close control over the price of drugs. However, I do know something about the situation and I shall give the hon. member the information as well as I can. The function of this department with

Food and Drugs Act
regard to drugs is to control their potency and purity. We have standards, usually international standards, which are enforced rigorously through sampling drugs through purchase at retail as well as through obtaining them from the manufacturers and wholesalers. This is done by spot sampling as well as by taking whole shipments of certain drugs. They are analysed by the department's officials, and if anything is wrong with them or if they do not conform with the pharmacopoeia requirements, they will be rejected and appropriate action will be taken. Therefore we do control the purity and potency of drugs. We generally get splendid cooperation in that respect from the manufacturers and the trade.

With regard to penicillin, this drug, as everyone knows, came into existence in consequence of the work of a great number of scientists and others, of whom the principal was Sir Alexander Fleming. It came into commercial production early in the war, in the United States first. In Canada it was and still is made, I understand, in three factories. The first is the Connaught Laboratories in Toronto. This institution is, as I recall it, the joint enterprise of the university of Toronto and the Ontario school of hygiene, in which the province of Ontario has an active interest, There the money necessary to put up the plant was expended by the federal government. Hon. BROOKE CLAXTON (Minister of National Health and Welfare) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a bill to establish a Canadian information service for collecting and distributing abroad information concerning Canada and to coordinate and assist the information service of the government and
Information Service

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: to provide for payment of salaries of staff and expenses of the service from moneys appropriated by parliament.

subtopic: COORDINATION OP AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: Is the minister going to explain the purpose of the resolution?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: COORDINATION OP AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext:
I shall be glad to do that, either now or later. It was the hope of the government that we might have first reading of the bill and then have it distributed. We would then take up the estimates of the Canadian information service, at which time h-on. members could secure full information about its operations, and proceed with the second reading of the bill at a later time. That seems to be the logical way to proceed.
In reply to the hon. member for Kamloops I would say briefly that the Canadian information service was established on September 28, 1945, by order in council P.C. 6300. It succeeded the wartime information board, which had been set up on September 9, 1942, by P.C. 8099. The wartime information board succeeded the directorate of public information which was brought under the Department of National War Services by P.C. 3333 on July 19, 1940. That succeeded the committee of public information which was established on October 7, 1939 by P.C. 2654 and by P.C. 4073 of December 8, 1939. The heads of these services were successively Mr. Walter Thompson, of the Canadian National Railways; Mr. Herbert Lash, of the Canadian National Railways; Mr. Charles Vining, of the newsprint export manufacturers association; Mr. John Grierson, Mr. A. D. Dun ton, and the present head, Mr. G. F. Andrew, to all of whom we are indebted for distinguished service during war time.
The purpose of the Canadian information service is much more limited than that of the wartime information board or its predecessors. Its purpose as set out in the order in council is to provide means and facilities for distributing information abroad concerning Canada and to coordinate and assist the public information services of the government. That purpose was amplified by the acting Prime Minister, after P.C. 6300 had been tabled, when he said-

subtopic: COORDINATION OP AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: What date was that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: COORDINATION OP AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext:
That would be immediately after September 28, 1945. He said:
Those with whom we trade must know our country and its possibilities; those with whom we associate for the maintenance of world security must know with whom they are cooperating and what may be expected of our cooperation. _ In short, both trade and diplomacy to be carried out successfully need a background of understanding based on factual information objectively presented.
At a later date I will, if requested, outline the way in which information services were developed during and after the war, in other countries as well as in Canada. I know of no country in which a similar service is not set up under one form or another, and in every country that I know of the service is set up on a much more elaborate scale and at greater cost than is intended for the Canadian service.
The aim is to establish a small service as compared with the service in any other country, to be under the immediate administration of the director, Mr. G. F. Andrew, but with regard to matters of policy and major concern to be subject to the supervision of a supervisory committee. On that committee would be representatives of other government information services, as well as representatives of the Department of External Affairs and the Department of Trade and Commerce. There would be a staff at Ottawa and their first function would be to provide for Canada's offices abroad, wherever and whatever the offices may be, information about Canada. That was found to be necessary to keep them continuously informed during the war, and it has been found useful, desirable and necessary in the post-war period. The information service takes several forms. It includes the distribution of books as reference libraries, and publications. It prepares reference papers on matters of current interest, such as for example, the situation as to food, Canada's trade, Canada's financial aid to other countries; and it sends out descriptive booklets as well as a regular daily air mail service, a weekly summary of news, and a monthly publication. In addition it supplies our offices abroad, through or in coordination with the national film board, with films, still pictures, and so on. It also, of course, answers inquiries received from abroad, and tries in every way possible to make Canada better known in other countries, the need of which is agreed to by everyone.
This information is sent to the officers of the Canadian information service at New York, Washington, London, Paris and Canberra. The material also goes to our diplomatic representatives in the countries of the British commonwealth and in foreign countries where we have representatives. It goes to the trade commissioners and other representatives, and officers of Canada stationed abroad.
I noticed in the Montreal Gazette to-day a dispatch on the front page on the introduction of this bill which certainly is intended to give every appearance of being a news dispatch. The byline is from the Gazette's resident correspondent at Ottawa, July 18. Then fol-

Information Service
lows what appears to be a news dispatch, but it has a serious misstatement of fact and several statements of editorial opinion. One of the things stated there is:
External Affairs has publicity men attached to many of its embassies and legations in other countries.
It states that therefore the Canadian information service is not necessary. The only publicity men, as they are called here, attached to embassies or legations are officers of the Canadian information service. External Affairs has no other public relations or information people in its service. When that is said it meets very largely the point which the Gazette correspondent or the Gazette itself tried to make.
Similar services are considered to be necessary by the United Kingdom, the United States, France, Australia, New Zealand and every other country that I know of. All the countries I have named have information representatives in Canada, at Ottawa or elsewhere. I have fairly full information about the size of the offices, the size of the staffs, and the amount of the expenditures of many of these information services of other countries. Of course we are anxious to set up this service, as economically as it could be done having regard to the needs of the Canadian people. I can assure the house that I know of no more modest service than that which we seek to set up,, and I know of none in which the salaries are more reasonable and the total over-all expenditure is as small.
I have dealt with the primary function of the information service. But it also has another function, and that is coordinating and assisting the other information services of the government in Canada. It has done that. Perhaps I should give a concrete example. There is an interdepartmental committee called the rehabilitation committee. It is furnished with a chairman and a secretary as well as with expert assistance by the Canadian information service. The food information committee is another example, and I could give others. That is the kind of thing that has been done by way of coordinating and assisting other Canadian information services.
The third function of the Canadian information service is to act in connection with Canada's attendance and participation in international conferences. It has been found by every country that it is desirable at all the major conferences to have attached to each delegation an information officer to arrange for press conferences, for the preparation and release of material to the press, for the preparation of background material, and that kind of thing, so as to ensure that so far 63260-228
as possible the reports of material of primary interest to the country concerned-in this case Canada and its citizens-are made continuously available by the delegation through the ordinary press agencies for distribution and dissemination at home. Such an information officer attached to a delegation is able to advise the delegation on presenting its material, on meeting the press, and on other questions sometimes quite technical, which things are necessary if a country is to secure an adequate dissemination of information about its position.
The fourth function of the Canadian information service is to act as the information bureau or supply the officers for the information bureau at international conferences held in Canada. I have in mind not only the two Quebec conferences but also the second meeting of the council of UNRRA, the meeting of the food conference, the meeting of PICAO and others, where the Canadian information service provided what was in essence the international staff necessary to discharge the informational needs of a great international conference.
Another function of the service is to arrange for foregin visitors to come to Canada and to see that as far as possible while in Canada they receive whatever facilities may be necessary to enable them to see what they want to see of our country. That kind of service is now furnished by every government. We have found it necessary to do it, and it is necessary that it should be done by a special service.
Finally there has been set up, as hon. members know, the united nations educational, scientific and cultural organization-UNESCO, as it is called-which was the result of meetings held at London in November, 1945. Canada signed the convention, and some sixteen countries have now ratified it. Canada no doubt will ratify it in due course, and it will be necessary then for some agency in Canada to act as the corresponding unit, the funnel through which there will be two-way communication between UNESCO and the proper agencies in Canada; and that will be partly the Department of External Affairs, and partly the Canadian information service.
The bill, which I hope will secure first reading, and will be distributed soon, is very much along the lines of the order in council setting up the Canadian information service, under which it has been working since it was set up some months ago. As I have said, it is the hope of the government that if first reading is secured for this bill and the bill is distributed, at once we shall move into committee of supply, and there I shall be glad indeed to deal with the estimates of the privy council which

Information Service

relate to the Canadian information service and answer all questions which hon. members may put.

In any event, it is not necessary for me to read the editorial. The criticism is that of a newspaper writer returning from England and therefore it was based on personal observation. The criticism was to the effect that the British people were under the impression that they were still getting the bulk of their bacon imports from Denmark, whereas in fact the bulk of those imports were coming from Canada. The journalist remarks-and his remarks were quoted-that it was a pity that the Canadian information service, which was spending the people's money, did not tackle that problem in realistic fashion to bring to the people not only of England but of the continent of Europe the great part which Canada was playing in con-

Information Service
tributions to UNRRA by way of food and financial relief. If have this service at all-and this is our first criticism-it is not discharging its functions in an efficient manner in the interests of Canada; in other words, the people of Canada do not get value for their money.
I hope the minister will not say that my suggestion means that we are urging him to spend more money. We are not, and we shall point out before we are through that we want a full explanation as to why it is necessary to spend as much as we are spending on this service and whether we need the service in its present form. However, that point is one that can be discussed later.
To our minds, the main question is whether the service is essential. We have various other departments of government with agencies in foreign countries, and we have departments of government here which operate bureaux in foreign countries, all of which spend money on advertising, public relations, and similar work abroad. This brings to mind the question whether we need to spend a large amount for a separate body under a separate minister to provide the same or a similar service. There are several general questions, and objections of a general nature which I think should be brought forward.
The minister listed several functions performed by the Canadian information service, some of them very unconvincing as arguments in support of the need of this service. I propose to mention several objections to and criticisms of the general idea of carrying on this service. In the first place, as the minister has pointed out, this is a descendant of a war-time service, the wartime information board, a service which was set up under emergency legislation and was presumed at that time to be intended to last only for the duration of the war. I suggest that the people of Canada were entitled to assume that the board would come to an end with the end of the war and that the money spent on that board would thereby be saved.
May I remark that the decision to continue this function, under the head of Canadian information service, is illustrative of the general trend which we have observed, whereby establishments set up to deal with emergency situations tend to become permanent. It is another illustration of the general trend of expenditures, instituted and justified on the grounds of emergency, becoming established, set and taken as a matter of course and so continued when the emergency has passed, and in fact even increased.
If we had in this country plenty of money to spend on old age pensions, plenty to spend on social security, and sufficient revenue to justify a cut in taxes, then the position would be quite different. But we heard the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) say that this group here had failed to suggest ways in which expenditures could be reduced. We heard him say that until we could reduce expenditures we could not reduce taxation. That in itself suggests the principle which the government should bear in mind in carrying on these services, and unless they suggest much more vital and important reasons than the minister has given this afternoon, we on this side will remain entirely unconvinced of the necessity of this service and of the justification for spending money on it.
I may interject here that the item in the estimates this year, at page 73 of the main estimates, amounts to $640,700. That is item 591. That means well over half a million dollars. On the face of it, we are not convinced that this service is essential or that the money that is spent can be justified. If it could be shown that the service bore a relation to vital policy which the government was concerned to put over in countries overseas, such as an immigration policy for the encouragement of immigration on any general scale, which could be called a policy, it would be a different matter, and still I should say that it would require careful proof whether a separate board was necessary under those circumstances. But we have had no proof that it is related to some specific purpose. We have had merely a general statement that it will assist other departments in the discharge of their existing functions.
In that connection, I would point out something in regard to which the house and the country should have some information. The Department of Trade and Commerce, as will be seen at page 51 of the main estimates, is spending $459,000 this year on trade publicity and advertising in Canada and abroad, and I should wish to be conclusively shown that there was no overlapping before I would suggest that we cease criticizing this large expenditure which we are asked to continue under this bill. The Department of Trade and Commerce is also spending $650,000 to assist in promoting tourist business in Canada. Possibly the minister can tell us how much of that is spent outside the country, for it is unlikely that all that money is spent in Canada. I should imagine that a good deal of it is spent in advertising abroad. However, that point can be covered later. Here at any rate we have $650,000 plus $459,000, or over a million dollars being spent
Information Service

by the Department of Trade and Commerce alone in advertising Canada or in assisting ;he tourist industry.
Then, in the Department of External Affairs we have an item for $2,436,325 for representation abroad. It may be that at present none of the persons paid by the money voted in that item is charged with responsibility for advertising Canada abroad, but I would suggest that these officials, together with the trade and commerce department, have an extensive programme in contemplation. It might be more efficient to give them the function of advertising Canada abroad, and we might discharge that function at the cost of a great deal less money than is involved in setting up a separate branch for Canadian information services and voting it over $600,000.
While we are on this matter, may I refer to a return which was tabled, being sessional paper 137 of March 15, 1946, in reply to a motion by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), who asked: (a) How much money was expended by us through the wartime information board, by years, while it was in existence? (b) How much thereof was paid to persons outside Canada, and for what, and who were those persons? The return shows that for the year 1942-43 the total spent by and through wartime information board was $1,473,524; in 1943-44, $759,000-1 am giving the round figures-in 1944-45, $1,700,000; in 1945-46, up to September 28, when the board was transferred to Canadian information service, $754,000. That represents a total in those four years of $4,687,267.39, of which, in the same period, a grand total of $37,456.49 was paid to persons other than Canadians. I put these figures on the record to show what has been the scale of expenditures in the past.
I should also like to refer to another sessional paper in which the question was asked as to the estimated monthly expenditure of Canadian information service

that is, the present service-and of what items that expenditure consisted. The answer was that the monthly expenditure was $53,714. So that we are spending $53,714 a month on what would appear to be on the face of it a questionable service. The necessity for it is questionable, and it may well be that the personnel could be replaced by other bodies already in existence.
Another objection which we have to this Canadian information service is that it is another of those government bureaux concerning whose activities we have experienced great difficulty in obtaining information. We have

had several instances of this sort in this house in the last day or two. I will not refer to them because they did not occur during this debate, but I can refer to something that took place in' connection with this very service last year, when the hon. member for Eglinton moved for a copy of all minutes of proceedings of the committee supervising the Canadian information service. What took place is to be found at page 2118 of Hansard of November 14, 1945. The minister refused to produce the minutes of proceedings on the grounds of privilege. The hon. member for Eglinton said:
I am not asking in the motion for the production of reports to the minister or for opinions given to him by this committee. What the motion asks for is a copy of the minutes and proceedings of the committee. If you look at the order in council referred to by the minister you will see that this is an administrative body. It is charged with carrying out the provisions of the order P.C. 6390.
I might point out, Mr. Speaker, that that order is in almost exactly the same words as the present resolution. The order read that the service was established for the purpose of providing "means and facilities for distributing abroad information concerning Canada and for coordinating and assisting the public information service of the government." I think the point made on that occasion by the hon. member was a good one. It was not a confidential document in the way of a report he was asking for; he was asking for minutes and proceedings of the committee after it had met in order that we might know what was the policy of this service. The hon. member went on to say at page 2119 of Hansard:
My next point in reply to the minister is that parliament has the right and the duty to know what the Canadian information service is doing and is planning to do, and the minutes of the supervising committee contain that essential information. Therefore they must be available to parliament, if parliament is to be in a position to do its duty.
The minister, however, supported by the Minister of Finance, then Acting Prime Minister, maintained his position. The matter was put to a vote in the house and the motion was defeated by the usual government majority, the vote being 85 to 105. Therefore I say this appears to be merely another of these government boards with regard to which parliament is to be denied information. On that ground I question very much the wisdom of continuing it, certainly the wisdom of setting it up by statute, until we are assured that the policy of the minister and the government in that respect has been changed.
There is one further objection which we have, and which is of a general nature, namely, that this service must bring to this country

Information Service
inevitably the dangers inherent in all government information agencies. I should like to speak, and would be expected to speak, fairly carefully here, because I know the persons in charge of these agencies are persons of good faith, and persons who attempt to act in good faith. But I submit in all seriousness that it is impossible for persons charged with disseminating information about government activities to avoid colouring their information constantly with items and points of view favourable to the administration whose policies they are publicizing. That is inevitable. If they did not do that they could not be maintained in office. There might be hon. members who say that such a trend is not dangerous, but I think most hon. members on this side of the house-and certainly all in this particular group-feel that that trend is an extremely dangerous one. Probably even if this party were in office the same trend would be evident, because as I say, the trend is inevitable in connection with government publicity. That is why we think government should keep out of the publicity business, not only on the grounds of expense, but also on the ground, if you like, that it is not justified in spending any public money for political or propaganda purposes- and propaganda cannot be avoided in this sort of activity. That is another reason why we resist the proposal to set up this service and perpetuate it under a statute.
That just about completes the objections we have to this board. In conclusion, I should like to emphasize the first point I made. The service might perform a useful function though we are not convinced of that. It might perform a useful function in so far as disseminating information overseas is concerned-I certainly think that should be the very limit of its function; it should disseminate no information in Canada. But we want to be convinced that it is performing that service, because it is essential that the people of Canada get value for their money.

subtopic: COORDINATION OP AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext:
The resolution of the minister states that it is expedient to present a bill to establish a Canadian information service. It is not expedient; it is a reckless raid on public funds. At the present time we have public ownership of railways; we have insurance companies, banks, departmental stores and other mercantile organizations, all supplying information abroad. They have their agents and all of that kind of thing. We have also Trade and Immigration, air and steamship lines.
When this information bureau started during the war it was used largely for political propaganda purposes. Information by the ton was sent out all over Canada, all over the
world and on the seven seas. But what did the editors of the newspapers do with it? Many of them said they threw it in the wastepaper basket. The information was not information at all. As I said before, the service should not have been created.
The resolution says that it is expedient; if it is expedient, it is not necessary. Is it expedient to be spending a billion and a half dollars on civilian estimates at the present time? Think of all the trips abroad! I fancy this department started in a small way. It was a reflection on the press which did such great work in the war. First, they got one clerk and then they borrowed a few fellows from the civil service. Then they launched out. They said, as Israel Tarte, the one-time member for Montmagny-L'IsIet, said, " Wait until you see us next year." Who are these people? Take up the main estimates and you find that every department of the public service has publicity agents abroad on the seven seas spending money like water with duplication and waste. There are all kinds of duplications. They are doing work that is largely the function of trade and commerce and industry. We have trade agents and immigration agents and all that sort of thing for eleven million people. We are overgoverned and overtaxed from one end of Canada to the other. No wonder the people are losing confidence in us as representatives. I said that when this matter was up a few years ago.
As John Hayden said in 1797, referring to the golden age:
The press is now the only organ of public opinion.
Much more than the House of Commons is. I continue:
This title it assumes; but it is not by usurpation; it is rendered legitimate by the defects of your parliamentary constitution; it is erected upon the ruins of real representation. The periodical press is the rival of the House of Commons; and it is, and it will be, the successful rival, as long as that house does not represent the people, but not one day longer.
These, wise words were used years ago, and they are correct to-day. Our parliamentary system, erected by the people, now looks to the press for its information, and they represent public opinion more than we do. When the information bureau was set up during the war, it was, as I then said, a reflection on the press. Instead of utilizing existing agencies, the government assumed the functions of the press and it was wide of the mark.
The minister is fond of spending money and duplicating services. I do not wish to reflect on him because he is an able young man, likable and fuli of promise, and an old friend of mine, but I object in the public
Information Service

interest to certain things in this matter, namely, the duplication and the waste which is going on in the public service of Canada. The provinces have information bureaux and picture books which they get out and send all over the country and the world. The various departments of provinces and municipalities are all spending money on publicity, or at least some of them are. They cannot spend it like water in the municipalities because the taxpayers have a check on them every December or January first in the annual elections. If they spent money like that they would be put out of office. This spending of money is all reflected in the federal tax rate. This extravagance will go on just as long as the House of Commons stands for it. The suggested expenditure for this new service should be reduced to $1, and then you would be spending a dollar you do not need to spend. It provides no information; it does not bring a soul to Canada.
The work done during the war in the information bureau along these lines was done by civilians who were established in good :at jobs, complete with travelling expenses by aeroplane, hotel bills, drawing rooms, and all that sort of thing. And they can simply snap their fingers at the auditor general. No wonder the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) is getting sick of it. The taxpayers are getting sick of it, too. People in the constituencies are wondering what kind of parliament this is, when it is so ready to spend money like water to maintain some of these useless institutions and services of no value.
This is not an expenditure in the public interest. We have seen the work done by the old government of Canada information bureau in New York, housed in a luxurious office, with all travelling expenses paid. They counted that day lost in the United States in which they did not spend at least $5,000 or $10,000 for fads and frills. Just look at the state of affairs in the United States, particularly in congress and in the senate when there was a debate about the loan to Britain. The Canadian information bureau was supposed to give information to the American people, to draw them away from their old type of history books which described a Britain of the Seven Years war, and all that kind of thing. That is the sort of thing the information bureau was supposed to be doing and to cure in New York and the United States.
Did the bureau change any of that information? No, they have the same old history books. I have seen them in Cleveland, Buffalo and other cities, with information in them equivalent, to the days of Lord North. That
[Mr. Church.1
is the kind of information they are still using and getting after this extravagant expenditure of money of ours there. The municipalities could not spend money like this, and the provinces have been curtailing their expenditures. There is no necessity for it, at all.
I believh it was in Cleveland, Detroit or Toledo-I am not sure which-where I saw a pamphlet and pictures of information describing those celebrated gentlemen of the Royal Canadian Mounted police, who are under the control of the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent). Americans come up here in front of the parliament buildings during the summer and see our splendid mounted police wearing their red coats and their military uniforms in this awful heat and making a laughing-stock out of parliament which asks these brave men and' the finest police service to wear them, in the idea that this sort of advertising is necessary to encourage people from the United States to come to Ottawa. We are spending money to advertise the mounted police, when they do not need advertising, at all. Their great record in peace and war alike does not need such publicity.
The time has come for a halt. Parliament is going to get a rude awakening at the polls when the next election comes along. If we look at the back of this book of estimates I have before me we find details of expenditures made in the public service. What right have we to open up new departments, when the war is over, and. to extend this service? New Zealand and Australia would not stand for it; the people down there would not put up with it. I doubt not that if the people of Canada had an opportunity to vote on it they would vote it down.
We shall have to strike out all these unnecessary post-war expenditures, and let us get back to a consideration of the interests of the small businessman, the taxpayer, the farmer and the artisan. I have had occasion to take note of the kind of advertising done by large department stores such as Eatons and Simpsons. They do ten times more work in a day than this fancy department of government would do in all the years since its creation.
I have always been against this method of advertising our country. Canada does not need to be advertised along the lines mentioned by the minister. The quicker we get back to striking these expenditures out of the estimates, all these fads and' frills, the better it will be for responsible government in this dominion. There is no such thing as responsible government here, anyway. We

Information Service
might as well pack up and go home, for all the control we have over expenditures. We have a comptroller of the treasury, but if he finds anything wrong under the War Measures Act we never hear about it. He is just holding postmortems after the money is spent.
There will be a day of reckoning after the next election. The undertaker will be there ready to provide accommodation for some of the politicians both in and out of the house who are willing to stand for expenditures like this.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: COORDINATION OP AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext:
It was an amendment which, among other things, supported the cooperatives, which my hon. friends voted against.
In expressing general support for this measure, I wish to make it clear that this does not mean that I do not agree with the contention of the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) that we should get full value for our money. I agree with him that parliament should know as much as possible of what is going on in the Canadian information service, and it is our job to do everything we can to keep those who are operating that service on their toes so that they will do a good job.
I wish, however, to make the point that in the society of to-day we need all the light and knowledge we can possibly have. We cannot have too much of it. The hon. member for Kamloops referred to this service as one which had been initiated during the war under
*the authority of the War Measures Act, and expressed the opinion that it had been an emergency measure which should have ended with the end of the war. My view is that there were many things which had their beginning during the war but which did not come to an end at its close.
It is possible that we may have learned a few things in those bitter years, and one of the things we learned was the great need for public information, and for our own people to know as much as possible of what is going on, and for the rest of the world to be fully informed about us. This might be considered as being in the field of adult education. We do not oppose the idea of provincial, or municipal governments sponsoring and providing education for our children. In our western democracies at any rate we have got past the stage where we feel that because governments are in charge of education of our children, necessarily such education is in the form of propaganda. Such is not the case.
Education does not stop at grade 8, grade 12 or with university. Surely it goes on throughout the whole of one's life. In a dynamic age, such as the one in which we are living, if we are to be able to live in it and to meet effectively the problems which arise from time to time, our people must continue to learn as long as they live. They must be supplied with all possible information about happenings in our own country, and trends and developments throughout the world. On that basis I feel it is one of the responsibilities of the government to organize an information service. Since this matter of public information is a new field I recognize immediately that the government is put in a difficult spot. I do not quarrel with the hon. member for Kamloops for pointing out the dangers of creating government information services. I do not agree with him, but I think it is well that the point was made, so that the government will realize that they must lean over backward, that they must be particularly careful, especially in getting started, so that the reputation of this service will not be ruined by its being just a propagandist agency; it should be set up to provide information in an objective way.
I remember a case in point two or three years ago when this matter was up in the house, I believe on the estimates of the wartime information board. At that time I joined in part with my hon. friends in complaining that too much of the material in some of the W.I.B. documents and pamphlets that were going overseas had to do with information about the government. I tried to make the point to the minister in charge-I believe it was the present
Information Service

minister who was then parliamentary assistant to the Prime Minister-that to give a true picture of the situation in Canada there should be some account of what the other parties in the country were doing as well as of what was being done by the party that happened to be in power.
There was a long battle and our request was refused on the floor of the house, but eventually we won to the extent that in the issue of Canadian Affairs published just before the election by W.IiB., the predecessor of the Canadian information service, there appeared statements which had been prepared by the national parties which were taking part in the election of 19'45. I do not think anyone was sorry that this was done, because it was a presentation of the picture as it stood.
I was glad to see a move made in the direction of getting away from the fear that you must not talk about political parties. After all, the}' are a large part of our national life. If you are to tell the story of what is going on, the story of the political parties has to be told. I felt encouraged that we had made some headway a few months ago when I was overseas attending certain international meetings. At that time the Canadian delegation was supplied by the Canadian information services with information as to what was going on back home in Canada. When you are away from home it means a great deal to get these telegraphic dispatches. I have a vivid recollection of feelings that, while the coverage was necessarily brief, nevertheless it was quite broad. I remember that almost all of one dispatch was devoted to an amendment that had been moved and the remarks made on the floor of this house by the leader of the group to which I belong. While my hon. friends to my right might not like that, it proved to me that the Canadian information service was trying to give a true picture of what was going on back home.
It would appear to me that there is more to the job that should be done by an information service than was referred to by the minister. He may have overlooked part of it, or perhaps I missed it, but as I understand it the job of a public information service is not just to disseminate information abroad; it should also disseminate information within the country. We still receive a good many documents from the Canadian information service, although not quite as many as during the latter months of the war or, if I may say so, just before the election. That may seem to defeat the point I am trying to make, but in fact it does not. I am in wholehearted support of the basic principle, but naturally I want to see

this service carried on in an objective way. When the minister speaks on this matter again when we are in committee I hope he will have something to say about the domestic phase.
We all recognize the importance of publicizing Canada abroad, and those of us who have had the privilege of attending international conferences will, I am sure, all subscribe to that. However, I am more concerned about the level of the information given to our people here at home. As I said, I think that should be the principal job of a public information service. I hope these people will be given all kinds of support. That will not mean that we will not criticize them if we think they are not giving full value for the money spent; it will not mean that we will not criticize them if we think they are giving too much publicity to what the government is doing and failing to recognize the other activities in the community. With these and other suggestions that we might make later on, I want to support strongly the idea of developing and strengthening a public information service.
We are all aware of the difficult and trying period through which we have gone in the last six or seven years, yes in the last ten or fifteen years, but my notion is that we shall have even more difficult times ahead of us. One of the ways to fortify our people and help them to understand and adjust themselves to changing social and economic conditions, to understand problems-in the international field, is to have as much knowledge and information as possible. I contend that it is one of the responsibilities of a democratic government to organize an information service among its people.
I know that every time this kind of thing is brought up people say, "It is being done by the government of the day." I do not support the government of the day-I did my best in April, May and June of 1045 to see that they were not returned-but this is a democracy. Hon. gentlemen opposite are there by the will of the people of this country; while they are there, it is part of their job to let the people know what the various departments are doing.

When this service is set up by statute I should like to know under what minister it will operate. The wartime information board came under the privy council and I believe the estimates are still under that department in the demobilization section. subtopic: COORDINATION OP AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before this resolution carries I should like to make a few observations that occur to me as being important in connection with the Canadian information service. I was interested in what my good friend, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), just said with respect to the Canadian information service conveying to the public information concerning the work being done by the respective departments of government. I would not think so much of that except for this: In the minister's own department, if my arithmetic is correct, either the Canadian information service is not doing the job it was intended to do, or else the minister is duplicating that service on his own, because I find that altogether $518,000 is being spent by his own department on publicity and information.
It is difficult, Mr. Speaker, to criticize governmental policy and administration without seeming to reflect upon those who are employed by the government in carrying out its policy. But I want to make this clear, that in the Canadian information service are many exceptionally able men, quite a number of whom I know myself, but under the present set-up of the Canadian information service these men are simply being encouraged by the government to waste an important part and the productive part of their journalistic life. I do not think many people-I want to put this baldly in clear language-are going to be fooled by the set-up of the Canadian information service. There are some practical people in parliament whom it is not easy to fool. You can picture the Canadian information service in any way you like, but the natural trend of such a service is not simply to convey information about the departments of government, but in the last 63260-229
analysis it becomes a propaganda machine for the government that happens to be in office. Let us look that fact squarely in the face and not be fooled by any fancy language concerning it. Actually the Canadian information service should not be called the Canadian information service. It should really be called the Canadian government perpetuation service, because that is what the service eventually becomes in effect. Again I want to make it clear that it is no reflection on the men who are in this service, for many of whom I have the highest regard both personally and for the ability they so often exhibit. This information service is not even a fifth wheel to the parliamentary coach; it is an eighth or ninth wheel, and unless the minister is able to make a much better case than he has done up to the present, I cannot see how this money is being spent to good advantage in the interest of the public at large. * Take the matter of Canadian news in United States newspapers. We have excellent men in the Canadian information service at New York and other places in the United States, but the whole policy of this government with respect to information is, in my opinion, misguided. I would ask the minister this question. Is he satisfied that in United States newspapers we are getting a fair share of Canadian news? I ask that question because, if we are to spend money on a Canadian information service over in the United States, we have a right to ask for some results. I know it may be said that in broad matters of advertising it is hard to lay your finger on results, but the one thing that strikes every Canadian visiting in the United States is the great lack of Canadian news in United States newspapers. There is hardly anything about Canadian business or Canadian affairs at all. The United States is a great country *which, of necessity, is interested in its own affairs, although it is interested in ours too. I do not think the minister will be able to show, even though we have this great Canadian information service covering the United States, that it is contributing to the spreading of Canadian news abroad any more than the ordinary newspaper services. Indeed, sometimes I feel that the setting up of this information service is a reflection on the regular news services which did such a good job in Canada and the United States in the war and in peace. If this Canadian information service is not for the purpose of duplicating the ordinary news services, then it falls into a category of its own, the category which I have suggested, where it must eventually become simply a perpetuation service of the government in power.

Information Service

We have moved far away from the olden days when political parties used to try to get their own publicity across to the people. Now, if you are the government, you do not have to spend your own money for political purposes; you spend other people's, even the money of those who are trying to put you out of power. That results in an impossible situation.
You may have the very best kind of men in the Canadian information service; but, after all, everybody is human, and who is it that pays the men in the Canadian information service? Is it the opposition? Is it the C.C.F.? Is it the Social Credit Party? No, it is the government. And who is it that has the right to hire and fire these men? Is it the opposition? Is it the C.C.F.? Is it the Social Credit Party? No, it is the government. There is not a practical businessman in this parliament who does not know that those who have the right to hire and fire have some little say at all events in how you shall do your work. We might just as well tear the mask off this whole thing and show it in its proper perspective. In doing so, I suggest to those connected with this service that they take what has been said here as a warning that in the years to come they may find themselves drifting into a position which they do not desire, of finding themselves part and parcel of the government.
My good friend, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, a few moments ago spoke of the scarcity of information published other than that which has to do with the government. I remember that in the war, judging by what was published, one might get the idea that only those who supported the government had anything to do with the war at all. There was one exception, a pamphlet, which contained a symposium on education to which both the minister and the leader of the C.C.F. party made admirable contributions. I was not at all satisfied with my own contribution, but they published it, perhaps for that very reason. That was the only occasion in the whole war, so far as I am aware, on which a government information bureau even mentioned that the opposition and other parties were sharing in the war effort. I am not going to blame anybody for that, because human nature runs through all political parties. Sometimes it is said that human nature differs with different political parties, but I have never been persuaded of that; and having the money in their hands, having the power in their hands, and having such an instrument as the information service in their hands like the government had, it would be too much to expect of human nature that they would not use it. I point

that out, because it seems to me to go to the root of this whole matter of publicity and information. The government are trying to sell themselves, and by artificial means. There is one sure way for the government to sell themselves, and I am not satisfied that they are doing it very well just now. Let them have a policy which meets the wishes of the people and carry it out, and they will not need all this information, which is paid for by people, many of whom do not support them.
In conclusion, I had hoped that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would not have supported the expenditure of this money, although I am, in a way not surprised that he did. I wonder whether the government realizes that the group sitting to my left regard them quite differently from the way they regard themselves. I believe the ideas of the C.C.F. are completely erroneous, and I hope and believe that what they have in mind will never come to pass. But they regard the present government as a sort of group of political John the Baptists, paving the way for something which is coming later, though let me add- that there is no comparison of any sort between the two sets of circumstances. But I hope the government will come to its senses some time and realize what it is doing. I hope I can lay it down as a general principle, agreed to, I trust, by all hon. members, that they recognize that Canada has reached the stage in her development and in her status, and the world has reached the position in which we are required to have instruments abroad for extending information about Canada. It must be accepted that everyone in Canada would like to see people abroad in other countries have more information leading to more knowledge, more understanding and more good will about Canada. I believe everyone will agree with that. I think they would also agree that, in view of developments in the machinery for intercourse with , other nations and of the materials for public opinion, something more is needed than we had before the war. meroe is that in order to perforin such a service you should have technical knowledges, skills and experiences which are not ordinarily to be found in the Departments of External Affairs and Trade and Commerce. That is, it is desirable that we should have a group of people who are journalists, people having journalistic experience, a group of people who have had editorial experience and who have general publicity or educational experience, as well as artists and writers. [Mr. Claxton.l

As a result of joint investigation by the army and War Assets Corporation, I am in a position to inform the house as follows:
1.	That no footwear was placed on the Point St. Charles dump by any army installation or by War Assets Corporation.
2.	A check on army vehicles has revealed that nothing but ashes and garbage was carried to Point St. Charles dump between May 1 and June 10, 1946.
3.	Mutilation of condemned footwear has not been army practice since 1941.
4.	All surplus army footwear is disposed of through War Assets Corporation, and at no time has such material been disposed of otherwise.
5.	That a major proportion of surplus army footwear is handled at the Valleyfield depot of War Assets Corporation.
6.	Canvas shoes which are found by qualified inspectors to be fit for further use are reconditioned as necessary and sold in the main to international relief agencies.
7.	Canvas shoes which the inspectors find are not fit for further use, and cannot be repaired, are sold as scrap.
8.	Used leather boots and shoes are examined by the inspectors and repaired if at all possible, but if mot repairable are sold as scrap.
9.	No canvas or leather footwear which is received in a repairable or usable condition by the corporation is scrapped by the corporation.
10.	It has been determined that the only surplus government footwear which could have been placed on the Point St. Charles dump was that sold by the corporation as scrap leather to private interests, who after investigation and examination of their purchase, decided that the cost of salvaging by separation of the various component material would be greater than the revenue that could be derived from the sale of these materials. Apparently the private interests decided to accept the initial cost as a loss and dumped the footwear.
