speechtext:
The house resumed consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Clax-ton-Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.
That it is expedient to present a bill to establish a Canadian information service for collecting and distributing abroad information con-verning Canada and to coordinate and assist the information service of the government and to provide for payment of salaries of staff and expenses of the service from moneys appropriated by parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose I was answering some of the questions that had been asked and some of the comments that had been made by some hon. members and was trying to show why it was considered necessary to set up an information service to do work which I think every one admits should be done in order to ensure that Canada shall receive adequate presentation abroad. I said that it had been considered that this should not be part of the functions either of the Department of External Affairs or of the Department of Trade and Commerce, first, because it needed people having special and particular qualifications and, second, because it had been found that the members of this service, not being members of the diplomatic corps, were able to maintain relations with members of the local press and others which enabled them to discharge their informational functions more effectively than could be done by members of the ordinary diplomatic services.
I would point out that the officers of the Department of External Affairs and of the Department of Trade and Commerce who are located abroad are already hard pressed and fully occupied with their own particular functions. It is quite evident from the examination we have made that it would not be possible for the offices of these two departments in the main centres to render additional service without the appointment of additional officers. Of course both departments do work alpng
Injormation Service

informational lines, and I think anyone who knows anything about the quality and calibre of the people representing Canada in External Affairs and Trade and Commerce will admit that they are doing admirable work. That is recognized by everyone and by the peoples of other countries.
We do not appoint special information service officers or set up a separate office unless there is a real need which cannot be met through these two departments. This has been found to be the case in New York, Washington, London, Paris and Canberra. In those places the officers of the Canadian information service are definitely subordinate to the senior officer of the Department of External Affairs and work very closely with him. I should like any hon. member who has visited New York, Washington, Paris, London or Canberra and who has seen what the representatives of the Canadian information service are doing in those places to tell us in what respect they have not done valuable work, work which needed to be done in the interests of Canada, work which should be done either by them or by the diplomatic representatives but which to be done by others would require the appointment of additional staff.
I should like to hear about that, because I have been concerned with this for two years and I have heard nothing but praise about the work these officers who represent Canada abroad are doing. I have heard no complaints except that they do not have enough money to do an adequate job and do not have an adequate staff.
These officers have been chosen solely with a view to their suitability for the positions they occupy. Some reference was made by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) to the luxurious offices in New York. I dare say that those so-called luxurious offices have been visited by many hon. members and by many representatives of the press. We have heard from them-when I say "we" I mean the Canadian information service for which I am speaking-nothing but praise. I have not heard of any complaint about the offices or services rendered. I think if anyone goes to those offices he would find that they are modest, . that they are rather overcrowded but equipped to do an adequate job along the lines I have indicated.
The person who set up the office in New York in the first place was Mr. Harry Sedge-wick, managing director of CFRB, a gentleman not known generally to be a supporter of this party. I think he did an excellent job there. He carried on through the years of the war and when the war reached a state

where he thought he could return to his own business, he did do. In Washington we had Mr. Hugh Campbell, the public relations officer in Winnipeg for the Canadian Pacific Railway company, now public relations officer everywhere for that company. He did a notable job in Washington, not only for the Canadian information service but for the armed forces and the people of Canada. I have never heard that he was an active supporter of the Liberal party or of any party.
I should like to deny with all the vehemence possible the charges which are implied or stated by hon. members or by others outside that there has been any sign of political propaganda about any of these activities at any stage. I think it is remarkable that in the course of this debate there should have been ' such references and insinuations without a single, solitary instance being given of any case where it has happened. That a country should have carried on an information service through one means or another from 1939 to this date, with no proof of that kind of activity ever being brought forward and supported, is a remarkable achievement and a great tribute to the people who carried on that service. It is also a recognition of the reality of the position as described by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre; that is, that a responsible government, which ours is, leans over backwards to ensure that nothing like that could possibly happen.
Was there ever a better example of this than when the Canadian information service met the request of the armed forces for information about the election and distributed to the armed forces overseas the issue of Canadian Affairs which described the aims and objects of the political parties.

speechtext:
The armed forces felt
that it was desirable in the interests of the men wTho wanted to vote in the election that information should be placed before them by the political parties. The Canadian information service, which published fortnightly Canadian Affairs, which ran through some fifty-six editions, and which did, I think, a notable job, was the vehicle chosen by which this might be done by the Canadian information service. The Canadian information service, looking at the precedents established in connection with the allocation of free time for political broadcasting over the C'BC network, called into consultation, just as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation had done in connection with broadcasting, representatives of the political parties in Canada which came within the general scope of the white paper regarding broadcasting which was issued in 1939, as brought up to date in 1944. That included the representatives of the political parties which had national offices in Ottawa. They were called into consultation. I am sorry that the party represented by the hon. member for Peace River did not come within that qualification at the time. It was no decision of mine or of the government's. It was decided on the basis of the test that had been laid down, and representatives of the Progressive Conservative party, the C.C.F. party and the Liberal party met and agreed on an allocation of space which roughly approximated the allocation of time for political broadcasting. It was done on that basis. The parties cooperated and as far as I know, they stuck to the rules which their representatives had agreed to or laid down.
The issue went overseas. It required a *tremendous feat of organization to get it into the hands of the troops in time. I can tell the committee this. I have heard from every side, irrespective of political affiliations, that the sailors, soldiers and airmen of Canada appreciated that service and regarded it as a fair way of treating them in the fairest election ever held in Canada in war time.

subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: The war is over.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext:
But I am answering a
remark that has been made, and I am not going to allow the fact that the war is over to enable people to make charges without
my being able to reply to them. I think the hon. member would want me to be allowed that privilege.
It was very interesting indeed to read that in the British House of Commons-I can give hon. members the reference-the question was raised why they could not do the same thing for the British forces because it had succeeded so well with the Canadian forces.
I will tell hon. members that never, either in my capacity as a member, fairly active in the ranks of the Liberal party, or as minister charged with the responsibility to parliament for the administration of this service, have I heard of any complaint from any source about the way in which that operation was carried on.
Apart from vague and general remarks and insinuations, I have never heard of any established case where it could be brought out that, this instrument of publicity and public information for the people of Canada has been used for partisan purposes. The hon. member for Peel, my very good friend, referred to the occasion when he, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and myself took part in a debate in Montreal. I must say that I thought, just as he did, that I got the worst of it on that occasion-

subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: I am quite sure I did.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext:
-because speaking as a supporter of the government as I was at the time I thought I had to stick closely to the constitutional and legal situation in which the federal government found itself. But I must say that, apart from that notice in Canadian Affairs to which he referred, I do not remember any issue of Canadian Affairs ever referring to the Liberal party doing this or to the Liberal party doing that. Also I do not think any official or officer of the Canadian information service thinks of his salary as being paid by the Liberal government of Canada. He thinks of himself as a servant of Canada; I think they all do and will continue to do so, just as we regard them. I think they have served the people of Canada exceedingly well during a difficult period.
So I feel that, in view of the fact that I do not know of any case which can be brought forward to support the assertions which have been made, this service has done an admirable work and done it in the interest of the people of Canada.
The hon. member for Vancouver South asked me to give an example of the way in which the Canadian information service worked, and then he wanted to know-and I wonder if he really regards his question as
Information Service

fair-how the Canadian information service endeavoured to place the viewpoint of Cana-,da before Russia.

subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: What is unfair about that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: It is recognized that it is exceedingly difficult for anyone to place any point of view before the people of Russia except through Russian agencies. I should say there that we send our representative in Moscow, our ambassador, Mr. Dana Wilgress, all the material there is. Also the government of the U.S.S.R. has in Canada its press agency which receives all the information that goes out to similar agencies.

subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: You mean, regular news agencies?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: Regular news agencies- Tass-and there is no other way that I know in which we could do it. I hope that answers the hon. gentleman's question.

subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: May I say a word? As a rule I do not speak very long. I was in Holland, a year ago this week, with the troops. They had just received a copy of Canadian Affairs. I was through the army headquarters, all the divisional headquarters and all around the various units there; and they were absolutely splendid in their appreciation of the issue of Canadian Affairs. I am not speaking now merely of Liberals, because most of those I met were supporters of my hon. friends opposite.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: Do not forget how they voted overseas.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: They said that was the finest thing done, that Canada was able to send over from all the parties an expression of their political philosophies and political ideals.

subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: Of course we are dealing with a set-up that is to be made permanent and carried on into peacetime. If the Minister of National Health and Welfare thinks the question about Russia was unfair, will he explain how this information service carries on its work, say in the Netherlands, or in Norway, or in Brazil?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext:
With regard to Brazil, we have in our ambassador, Mr. Jean Desy, a person who speaks now the language of the country, who is well recognized as being a very good representative of our country. He receives from the Canadian information service eveiy day the Canadian airmail bulletin; he gets our material weekly; he has been supplied with a library of books; he has his 
inquiries which are addressed day by day to the office in Ottawa, and promptly- answered, and he has also outlets for the kind of information which is furnished. In the case of Brazil a considerable quantity of the publications are issued in Portuguese, and Mr. Desy himself has been, I think, one of the most effective people in ensuring that knowledge of Canada is distributed abroad.

subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: In that case is the purpose largely to promote trade between Brazil and Canada, or what is the purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: Of course, to promote trade as well as to promote good relations in general. The trade commissioners who are there do their work in their own sphere, but they do not have the same opportunities of getting together information as have the people in Ottawa who are handling this service to send it to them and give them the means whereby they can carry on their work of representing us abroad. That applies both to the external affairs and trade commissioners in places like Rio.

subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext:
With regard to this matter I brought up in connection with the election service, since the minister has mentioned it I think I should clarify one or two points. We appreciate the service we got, and I think it did good. But what I was trying to bring before him was the inevitable position which it puts us in and puts the government in to have a service of that kind sponsored by the government. Let me make that clear.
We were not asked to sit in with the committee that allocated that time. It was known perfectly well that we had an organization, just as it was known that we had an organization in the case of CBC and the allocation of free time for political broadcasts from the CBC. Whether our office was in Ottawa, or Toronto, or Hamilton, or wherever it happened to be, we had a head office and an organization there. Therefore we should have been brought in. The first thing I knew about the matter was just a few weeks before the actual polling day, when I was sent a letter saying, " We are allotting your party 500 words in which to place your programme before the forces." I found that the allocation of time was on the basis which I mentioned this afternoon-500 words for ourselves; I do not recall what the C.C.F. had; the Progressive Conservatives were given between 1,600 and 1,700 words, and the Liberals between 2,100 and 2,200 words. If the Canadian informatien service used a formula arrived at by the CBC for the allocation of free time, I will say this, that the CBC now give as an excuse for the formula which was applied the fact that it was

Information Service
drawn up in a committee of this house. When we had a committee meeting a short time ago composed of representatives of the CBC and of all the parties in this house we found that no one on the government side was willing to change the allocation, because they claimed that the government should have a priority on the time, that they should have more time in which to broadcast to the people their policies and make representations with respect to those policies. I cannot quite understand why the minister cannot see this, that the position that the government are in inevitably, when they bring in a service of this kind and set it up, is that the people who come to the government for pay must take the position that the government is preferred, and they will take that position and will give them more space and more opportunity than they will give anybody else. That is only natural, unless the minister himself says to his Canadian information service, "We want you to be fair about this thing." If freedom of speech is to be tolerated in this country it must be free to everybody and equally free to everybody. That is the position we take. I have seen this type of thing worked before and I know the weaknesses of it. I know the minister himself has to take some responsibility, regardless of what he now says, that he did not have anything to do with it. The government did have something to do with it. Had the government stepped in and said, "We want this thing to be fair; we want the space to be fairly allocated," that is what would have been done. They did not do that, so that the Canadian information service would naturally say, "We have to give the government some preference in the amount of space." I do not see that they deserve any preference. Surely every political organization in the country that qualifies as a national political organization ought to have freedom of speech and freedom of publicity on anything which the government undertakes to do to get information to the people. If they are not going to undertake a service to get information to the people, well and good; we will take care of it ourselves, but if we are instituting a service let us institute it fairly and let it be free to everybody.

subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: During the recess there was brought to my attention by one of the citizens of Ottawa a matter which I had entirely forgotten, and I want to ask the minister a question with respect to it. Is it correct that one of those persons convicted of espionage was with the Canadian information service or the wartime information board; and, if so, who was that person?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: As far as I know, there was no one actually in the employ of the Canadian information service or the wartime information board who was connected with the espionage case or the report of the royal commission. There were two persons who had been seconded for a time from the armed forces for services in connection with the wartime information board and1 who there performed functions which were common to the wartime information board and the armed forces, but neither of them was ever on the strength or on the payroll of the Canadian information service.

subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: What positions did they hold? The minister indicates two. I heard of only one. What positions did they hold and how long tvere they with the wartime information board and the Canadian information service?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: I should preface this by saying that in this case there has not yet been an adjudication by the court. As hon. members know, Squadron Leader Poland was seconded1 from the Royal Canadian Air Force to the wartime information board, effective November 14, 1944 and was engaged in duties in connection with the board and the armed forces in the production of the Canada Digest. In May, 1945, his duties with the wartime information board ended. Prior to his undertaking these functions he was on the ordinary staff of the Royal Canadian Air Force at headquarters. Captain D. G. I.unan was seconded' from' the Canadian army to the wartime information board on November 6, 1944. He was attached to the information to the armed forces section where he was engaged in the production of Canadian Affairs. His period of secondment to the wartime information board ceased on February 28, 1946.

subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: I used the word "convicted". I presume these men are both still on trial and have not been convicted. I am not sure of the names and was only seeking information. In view of the fact that the matter was before the courts, I thought we should not discuss it inasmuch as it would not be justice.

subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext:
The minister mentioned that the ambassador to Brazil receives the airmail bulletin and that is how he helps to build up Canada in Brazil. I have here a copy of Monday, June 24, 1946, and I do not believe that any of this information is of much use to them in Brazil:
New army R.C. chaplain named. Brigadier Gibson heads M.P. 6. Colonel Bogart heads M.P. 3. Canadian merchandise exports decline. Births, deaths and marriages increase.
Information Service

There is a whole page of it and not a bit of it of any use to the ambassador there or to the people of Brazil. It is absolute bunk.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: The information contained in the airmail bulletin is not bunk. It is a report of events that happened that day, and of course different events take place from day to day. This bulletin is issued daily to all representatives of Canada abroad and its circulation totals 890 odd daily. It goes in Canada only to those who specially request it and have reason for asking for it. It is sent by air mail. The hon. member for Peterborough West suggested in his previous remarks that it is slow, that the ordinary sources of Canadian news are sufficient to carry the news contained in it. Well, this bulletin goes to fifty-two countries or colonies in which very little Canadian news is received. In none of them is there such regular news as that given in the airmail bulletin. It is sent by air mail because that is the most expeditious way of forwarding it without the cost of cable. Let me ask the hon. member whether in Brazil, for example, or in China, or in any of the other countries, except perhaps the United Kingdom and the United States, there is anything like the same news provided as quickly about Canada as is contained in the air mail bulletin. It is a succinct summary of news of each day. It contains no editorial opinions, nothing but bare news, and the news of course varies from day to day.

subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: This airmail bulletin is of use only to ambassadors or consuls in the different countries, the persons who really write and ask for it, and the information that is contained in the bulletin is not exactly what those people want. They would get better information from the Department of Trade and Commerce, and that department has its own bulletin and employs its own men to get out its information. Through the Department of Trade and Commerce information is supplied throughout the world and that is what these people want. They do not want the stuff contained in an airmail bulletin of this kind. This is only a sample. All the others that I have seen are exactly the same. The minister says that some are printed in French, but the people in France do not want them. Others are printed in Spanish. But who is going to read them in the Argentine, where Spanish is spoken, or in Chile, or Columbia, or Ecuador, or Peru.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext:
This bulletin is sent to Canadian representatives abroad so that they may keep continuously informed in a summary way about events at home and they get

news much more quickly than through any other source. It is also for the convenience of those who wish to pass on the news to people who speak some other language. These bulletins are designed primarily for the information of the people who represent us abroad, but it is given in a form which enables them to use it in passing it on to others who may be interested in the particular subject. The hon. member says that he finds the particular number to which he refers of the character that he has described. I receive these bulletins regularly, and I know they contain as accurate and succinct a summary of essential Canadian news as it is possible to draw up. They go out and are appreciated by officers of the Department of External Affairs and of Trade and Commerce and by the Canadian information service officers and any other officers of the Canadian service abroad.

subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext:
In my opinion a bulletin of ' this kind sent out by the Department of Trade and Commerce in cooperation with the Department of External Affairs would give information that was worth while to people in those countries instead of giving local news such as we find here. For example, I saw this item in the Montreal Gazette of this morning with reference to this resolution:
External Affairs has publicity men attached to many of its embassies and legations in other countries, and Trade and Commerce properly has such services to help promote foreign trade. There are Canadian publicity people in many parts of the world already, and there is no need for more.
I agree with the article in that paper.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext:
Earlier in the day I referred to the Montreal ..Gazette's news report from Ottawa with the editorial comment. The Department of External Affairs has no publicity officers abroad except those supplied by the Canadian information service. The Department of External Affairs and the Department of Trade and Commerce are represented in the advisory committee of the Canadian information service, and I should also add that they are represented on the working committee. There is a working committee set up with representatives of the publicity branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce. Its exhibition commissioner and its tourist bureau and the national film board and the CBC international service are on this working committee. They meet every week to work out the coordination of material which should be sent out and the coordination of activities. They work together in the closest possible way. Only to-day I was told that there are a number of communications

Information Sendee
by telephone and by personal interview between these three every day. If we did not have the Canadian information service providing the service for External Affairs, the Trade and Commerce officers and other officers of the Canadian government I feel, and I think the committee will agree, that it would have to be provided in some other way. It seems to us to be most economical that it should be done by one central service rather than by a variety of services. That does not mean that External Affairs do not send to their officers abroad special information related to external affairs. It does not mean that Trade and Commerce do not send to their officers abroad special information on general matters relating to Canada as a whole. The Canadian information service, working with External Affairs and Trade and Commerce, sends out the material.

subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: It might be cheaper to send out the Globe and Mail.

subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext:
I should like to follow that up in relation to the questions which I asked the minister and on which he spoke before six o'clock, namely, the relation between these services and the two departments of External Affairs and Trade and Commerce. In reply to that question, the minister said it was felt that we must have personnel abroad giving information about Canada. He said he thought the committee would agree with that general statement in the light of present circumstances and present development in the world. Perhaps I would be inclined to agree with that statement, subject to one important qualification, namely, that the object in mind in giving information about Canada was related to some specific government policy; as I say, policy perhaps calculated to encourage immigration into Canada. We see no evidence of such policy. If it be policy calculated to foster Canadian export trade with a certain country or groups of countries, then I submit that that policy could be better furthered by the Department of Trade and Commerce. Or if it be policy calculated to improve our ambassadorial relations with other countries, then I suggest that that policy could be better furthered by the Department of External Affairs. Unless the desire to disseminate information about Canada is related to some specific gavemment policy, we submit that this is an extravagance which Canada can afford to do without.
If the object of maintaining this Canadian information service is designed to improve our external relations or o\ir export or import trade, what department is better qualified
to do these things than either the Department of External Affairs or the Department of Trade and Commerce? Surely the minister does not suggest that the ambassadors, high commissioners and the first, second and third secretaries of the Department of External Affairs live in a vacuum and do not know anything about Canada and are not qualified to disseminate information about Canada; or that,the Department of Trade and Commerce, which at this very moment is running courses particularly to train young men and women who have returned from overseas, to teach them about Canada, its people and its various provinces, and all its aspects- not just trade-is not qualified to disseminate information about Canada. The Department of Trade and Commerce is spending a lot of money on teaching these people these things, and the department has a publicity branch which surely is qualified-if it is qualified to do anything-to send information overseas to the trade commissioners who go there.
The work of carrying out the objects which the minister has put forward in justification of the setting up of this service could be done a great deal more cheaply by utilizing the media of the already established departments. It would be cheaper to do it in that way than to set up a separate service which must inevitably duplicate and overlap the services that are being carried on by the two departments I have mentioned. That is the whole point. If we want the Departments of External Affairs and Trade and Commerce to exist in a vacuum, then, of course, we should make an attack on their estimates; but if we do not want them to exist in a vacuum which we do not, then I suggest they should take over the function which the minister has outlined as being the responsibility of the Canadian information service, and which they can discharge a great deal more cheaply and probably a great deal more efficiently.

subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: With all deference, are there not some ideas in my statement on which the minister should make some comments?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext:
I have already dealt with it before and after six o'clock, and said that close considerations were very much in the minds of these people who had to decide on whether or not the Canadian information service should be carried on separately by External Affairs and Trade and Commerce, each working in its own way, or by some agency in which they were both represented. It seems to me that the hon. member for
Information Service

Kamloops has made out a very good ease for doing it as a coordinated activity, and that is the way-

subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: Then cut down on the estimates of the other two departments.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext:
No, if you do not do it in this way you would have to add to the estimates of the other two departments if you wanted to have the service performed. We believe that there is a large desire to see that service performed; there is general need of seeing it performed. Somebody must do it and it seemed to us to be the most advisable way to do it. I can assure the hon. member that the supervisory committee with the representatives of External Affairs and Trade and Commerce, who are usually the under-secretary of state and the deputy minister, and the working committee with other representatives from each department

and the working -committee meets at least once a week-secure the most effective coordination and cooperation. If they saw there was any better way of doing it they would be glad to do it-they would have done it. But neither they nor the government as a whole have seen a better way of doing it.
May I say just a word further about the cost of a service of this kind. The amount sought in the estimates this year is $640,700 for Canada. In the United States estimates for similar services have been passed to the amount of $24,584,778; in the United Kingdom, $30,598,107; in Australia, $1,419,380; in Brazil, $2 million; and in the Netherlands, $S64,000. I do not mention these as indicating that we should necessarily spend the same sum. We are not spending anything like comparable sums on a per capita basis, particularly having in mind our widespread interests. But I mention it to indicate that in other countries people who are occupied with similar responsibilities have decided that very much larger sums, in comparison, should be spent on similar services.
If I might just answer an observation which was made earlier, namely that which suggested that these services should be on a fair basis within Canada, these services are designed primarily to extend beyond the boundaries of Canada. They are not aimed directly to do anything to affect public opinion in Canada. The services within Canada are those of coordination and assistance to existing government departments. The service is primarily designed for the dissemination of knowledge and information about Canada outside the boundaries of our own country.
[Mr. Claxton 1

subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: Following up the question I asked before, if, as the minister has said, it is the desire to coordinate the external work of the Department of External Affairs and the Department of Trade and Commerce, why was it decided to put the work of this coordinating committee under a separate minister, namely the Minister of National Health and Welfare? Is it possibly because he is the minister of propaganda for the government; or what good reason can be advanced for that decision?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext:
I very much resent
the suggestion that I am minister of propaganda for the government. I do not think the hon. member means that, seriously.

subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: I would not be surprised if he did.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: Well, then, I would ask the hon. member to withdraw it.

subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: I will not withdraw until I am proven wrong in making that suggestion.

subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: I was on my feet once or twice, Mr. Chairman. You saw me, but I did not want to break continuity of argument. I agree to a great extent with the arguments of hon. members who have preceded me. Personally, I cannot see why the Department of National Health and Welfare should have to care for an institution known as the Canadian information service.

subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: They are looking after it because it is sick.

subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: What is it that we have to make known through this information service? Surely we do not require it in Canada. WTe have our daily press and our periodicals.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: And our pulpits.

subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: We have radio stations, and our own Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: Our pulpits and our pews.

subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext:
These institutions disseminate all the information we need at home. What is the purpose? The purpose must be that we like to send information abroad, but what information do we have to send abroad? It is very nice to establish friendly relations with other countries, and I agree that that should be done, because we want to be friendly with other countries, and we have a shortwave broadcasting station at Sackville from which we give a world service for that purpose.

Information Service
So far as I can see, the only thing we have to let other people know is what we have to sell. If we want to advertise to the world that we have a big wheat crop and are looking for customers, all well and good. That is something which would come under the Department of Trade and Commerce. If we want to advertise Canada as the happy hunting ground for tourists, that would come under the same department. If we have anything to sell, the same is true. I am not going to make any charges or accusations; but I am suggesting that the Canadian information service will go beyond making known what Canada has to sell to the rest of the world.
I was interested in the speech made by the minister, [DOT] a speech which evidently was prompted by the hon. member for Peace River, the leader of this party. I was interested to note that when the minister was discussing matters requring the use of the expressions "divergence of views" or "controversial subjects", somehow- or another he seemed to have the mentally cramped view that those subjects of a controversial nature all exist within the confines of political partyism.
That is not so. He seemed to advance the argument that the organization now to be known as the Canadian information service had no more interest in Liberal policies than in those of other parties. Personally I am not greatly interested in that, because so far as I am concerned there are only two philosophies in the world.
I do not care particularly what party a man belongs to; if he disagrees with some other party I will guarantee that that disagreement is on methods of administration and not on ultimate objectives, or deep-seated policies and principles. There are only two philosophies in the world, one of which is the philosophy of free men, always recognizing the freedom of the individual and the principle that every man should be established in his own right without interference from any other person, body or government. That is one principle. The other is the philosophy of world statism.
I do not know whether the minister would be prepared to make comment on this point, but I say that when any information service, public body or radio deals with ways of life it must deal with one or other of those two philosophies. As a Canadian people believing in British democratic institutions-and I use the term "British" because I believe we do hold to those great Christian virtues-will the minister guarantee to the house that a Canadian news service will not propagate anything to the contrary view? I do not think he will.
Will he say that his Canadian information service will not at times give out information on Canada's foreign policy? Will he say that they will not? Let me say that you cannot write or think or speak foreign policy without advocating one philosophy or the other. That is why I wanted the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to make a few pronouncements the other day before leaving for the peace conference.
I am not concerned with Liberalism or Conservatism or socialism or social credit, but I contend that the minister holds one or the other of the philosophies I have mentioned, *whether he is a Liberal or anything else. I will almost guarantee that the foreign policy of the Minister of National Health and Welfare individually is no different from the foreign policy of the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell).

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext:
It must be a good
policy if they both agree on it.

subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext:
I am not debating the merits of the policy. You cannot say that one is a Liberal policy and the other a C.C.F. policy. I am not personally so much concerned over the Canadian information service boosting a party-of course I should like them to boost ours a little-but I do not think that is the danger; the danger is the propagation of philosophies for which the Canadian people do not stand.
Let me add one more word. This service is to cost well over half a million dollars. That may not sound so much since we talk in terms of astronomical financial figures, but half a millions dollars is a lot of money when you do not need to spend it. When the leader of the official opposition was speaking the other inght about cutting expenditures the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) asked where they could be cut. Here is half a million dollars. One of our biggest items of expenditure is in connection with the national film board and you could do away with that completely.
But I am not speaking only about cutting expenditures. We are setting up in Canada what I will call institutions for want of a better name, one of which is known as the Canadian information service. That is a nice name, but I a.m a little leery of nice names because so often we do not know what they really mean. This Canadian information service is being set up under a Liberal administration and it is gradually growing to enormous proportions. Then there is the Canadian Broadcasting corporation.
I am not going to be highly critical of these three institutions, provided that they are administered in the proper way. However,

there is no guarantee that Liberal administration is going to be in power forever-I hope they are not. There is no guarantee that the Conservatives are going to be in power. The Minister of Veterans Affairs has a habit of interrupting me. I would not mind that so much if he would only speak in English so that I could understand him. I sat back and said to myself, "I did not think we were living in such a wonderful country. How is it there is so much unrest if everything is so lovely?"
We are living in a time of unrest. If another government should come into office, either through the process of our democratic form of election or in some other way-believe me that is not without possibilities to-day-if a government holding to the philosophy of dictatorship should come into office the machinery would already be there for them to take over. What would be a greater plum for a dictatorship administration than the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation? The act governing this corporation would not need to be changed by one word. This new government would have this huge propaganda machine all ready for their own purposes. You would not be talking in terms of Liberalism or Conservatism or socialism or social credit then.
Another plum that would be ready to fall into their lap would be the national film board. This could be used to propagate what they would probably term the new order. Then we have the Canadian information service, one of the triplets of propaganda institutions which a government of that kind would find all ready for them. What would they say? They would say, "We did not bring them into existence; it was a previous government that prided itself on free institutions that brought these things into existence."	How often have I heard the
Prime Minister say over the years that he was here to protect free institutions.
That is the picture and we are spending millions of dollars on that type of machinery. I am not going to say that the national film board did not do some reasonably good work with certain films dealing with the danger

I suppose that the really effective Canadian information service at the present time consists of the members of this house. However, I want to turn now and make a plea to the minister on the basis of the Canadian information service being at the moment primarily for the dissemination of information abroad. speechtext:
The way it was put to me several times was that Canadians abroad working in our embassies are called upon- it is part of their job-to collect all the information they can about the countries they are working in, to send that information home ;o Canada. They would like to be treated n the same way. So far as they are con-:erned, they feel that, even though the departments here think they are sending them plenty of material, they are somewhat stranded. The hon. member for Peel will *[DOT]emember that the employees in the embassy
at Paris expressed that view to us, and they did so in other places we visited. I had the experience of being in Moscow during rather a. dramatic week, namely when the Prime Minister made a certain announcement in this country last February. I experienced with our diplomatic people there the sense of being stranded, and they said to me almost every day, "We are being asked to send home all kinds of information, but we do not know what is going on at home at all"; and as a matter of fact I was clear back in Canada myself before I knew anything about Canadian reactions to that particular incident.
I quote my own experience, brief as it was, merely in confirmation of the kind of plea that some of these people made to me, that they be given more information. I recognize that the Department of External Affairs has interests which keep it from doing as much of that job as it should, but here is a field for the Canadian information service. I hope they will realize that it is not just a case of giving news to these people over there; it is a case of increasing the effectiveness of our Canadian representatives all around the world, if they are given more information about what is going on back in Canada. I suggest to the minister that he be not afraid to give to these people through the Canadian information service at least a summary of opinions in Canada, a summary of editorials in newspapers of various political stripes. Just to confine it to factual material of the kind that has been read from a few samples to-night is not good enough. I come back to what I said before; I do not think we should be afraid of the word "politics". Political parties are a definite factor in our country, and these people have the right to a complete picture of what is going on.

subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext:
I can only approach this subject from the way in which I think, the average voter in Rosedale riding would look at it. When one sees an appropriation of $640,700 for the Canadian information service the question- immediately arises, do we need this service, and what does it do that would not otherwise be provided? When we remember that many a taxpayer is endeavouring to live out of his or her earnings-if single, * on $750 a year before reaching the taxation bracket, or if married, $1,500 a year, and I defy anyone to live decently in the city of Toronto on either of these sums, whether he be single or married, for it would be quite impossible-I believe that we should curtail a lot of our expenditures, no matter how necessary they are, until we can grant exemptions from taxation so that the government

Injormation Service
does not become an agency for lowering the standard of living of our people below what must be considered a minimum of decency. Then we find that the tourist business is going to spend 8650,000 in order to encourage tourists. That may be a justifiable expenditure because it brings in dollars and cents to Canada. But we find that this Canadian information service that is proposed to be set up is not concerning itself with trade and publicity, because there is an item in that department for trade, publicity and advertising in Canada and abroad of 8459,000, or an increase of $306,860. And here may I just say, that the Department of Trade and Commerce publishes an interesting little booklet, called "Canada, 1946", or whatever the year may be, which is an abstract of the Canada Year Book. This is a valuable book which not only gives information to Canadians, particularly to .students, but is also of extreme value to people from other countries who wish to get a bird's-eye view of what the industry and commerce of Canada is about. This book used to be made available to members at a cost of ten cents a copy. We had a man who looked after some economies, apparently, in this government. During the war years he took off the special rate to members, and if you want to buy a copy now to give away it costs you twenty-five cents. I believe that the government would be well advised to review some of the policies, even the policy of economy which in this case, I think, is false economy, and make this excellent and valuable book available to all hon. members, so that they may give it as wide a distribution as possible. I think I carry the judgment of the Minister of Trade and Commerce in this regard, but apparently no change has yet been made in the price.
What will my constituents think when they find that the rehabilitation information branch is to have 8242,000 appropriated for it, and the national film board, $1,030,683, and that is charged under "demobilization and reconversion", just why I do not know, the same way as Canadian information service is charged. Why it does not come under the ordinary peace-time estimates is another question on which the minister might give us some information. Then the national film board, in addition to the million dollars it gets under demobilization and reconversion, gets 8860,000 under the ordinary revenues. These are both items which many of my * constituents feel to be of doubtful value.
In regard to the whole matter of an information service run by the government, it is my belief, founded on some observations and information which I have received, that
the press generally in this country and abroad would much prefer to get their information at first hand, and not have the interposition of some special government department which "shades" the information and goes over it, censors it and dresses it up in the form which the department thinks is most appropriate, whereas trained newsmen are best fitted to give to the pubic that which the public wants to read about.
We have in this country, I believe, no ideology which we are trying to propagandize at the present time. The minister in fact resented the suggestion that, as being the responsible head of this ministry of information, he was in effect a minister of propaganda. That is another reason why I believe that what news there is about Canada should be left to the ordinary channels of publicity and not be given the imprimatur of the government or given any direction from governmental sources. Just where there is any actual dollars and cents advantage to be derived from an appropriation of $640,000 for the Canadian information service I do not know. It may be that it is an interesting and useful service to the department of External Affairs when our representatives are abroad, but it does not seem to me that having hourly or daily information about what is happening in the domestic field in Canada is exactly the reason why we send representatives abroad. They should have a knowledge of the broad problems of Canada, should know what the political trends are, if you like, and what the external policy of the country is; but who is in command of military district No. 3, et cetera, is not the type of thing which the taxpayers, in the constituency of Rosedale at any rate, are interested in funishing to our external representatives.
There is a limit to the taxpayer's burden, and he is already feeling that that limit is too high in view of the fact that we are no longer under the dire necessity of fighting a war for the preservation of our liberties. We think we are back in peace time, and we want to see some incentive restored to the people so that they can work, and work overtime if they desire, and in doing so obtain some benifit for themselves.
Canada's name has always stood high in the world and in the neighbouring republic to the south of us. It stood equally high if not higher in the days before we ever had an information service, and I fail to see how this particular department can be of use to Canada. If we are a first-rate nation and behave ourselves as we should toward our neighbours; if we are a good people, as we
Information Service

are, then our light will not be hidden, under a bushel; it will come to the surface and the world will recognize us for what we are. We do not need, therefore, any artificial information of this sort sent abroad for the purpose of publicizing our country.
There is news value in many of the government departments and the press are always eager to have releases, and do not wish to have the interposition of some agency which will tamper with and possibly dampen the effectiveness of that news. Information which the government puts out under such a department as this almost inevitably tends to become propaganda. The department may start out with the very best faith in the world and conduct itself along the, most scrupulous lines. But there is the inevitable human tendency to slant news a particular way in which one wants it to go, and it is my firm belief, and I believe the conviction of the majority of Canadians, that if items that are of news value in the country are given to our newspaper men-there are plenty of them,; our press gallery is full of able men looking for news-that is the best way to publicize the merits of the country. I suggest, therefore, that an expenditure of this kind can be done away with, particularly when the tax burden upon the people is so high.

I wish to direct to the minister two questions, one, having to do with service given abroad, and the second with the domestic service. With regard to the service abroad, am I fair in saying that this plan was hit upon early in the war to promote Canada's war effort, that we wanted to secure the greatest sympathy possible from the United States, and wished also to give the fullest information to Great Britain concerning our war effort and to inform other members of the commonwealth of that effort? Later on, it developed into the work of promoting the cause of the allies in the nations that were not at war. That was the genesis of the work abroad and, as hon. members know, the body charged with this work was called the wartime information board. It clearly was intended for wartime purposes. Now, having come to the end of the war, the government is trying to change direction, to find some new work for this information service to carry on, and as a result we have the plans that have been outlined by the minister to-day. With regard to the service abroad, it was designed primarily, in fact entirely, for the war, and now there is an attempt to build up something new for

peace. I would ask the minister to say whether I am fair in summing up the situation in that way.
With regard to the domestic service, the minister has pointed out that the work is to coordinate the publicity of different branches of government. That means, it seems to me, that this information service must be the top-dog, that it must be in charge of publicity services given by the different departments. I should like to know whether that is so. Otherwise I do not see that the service can accomplish a great deal. It would be interesting also to know how many persons there are on the staff of the service at the present time, how many of them are abroad, how many in Canada, and what the plans are for the next year with regard to staff.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: The hon. member for Vancouver South suggests that .this activity was created in time of war. That is obvious; and, as he said, it was primarily designed to improve the knowledge of Canada abroad and to create an understanding among the allies and to cooperate to the best possible advantage. I think it did that very well and worked together with other information sendees to that end. But, the hon. member says, with the close of the war now, there is an effort to find some new work for this agency which was created in war time. May I say with respect that that is not so at all. It would have been very easy indeed to disband this activity, had it not been found that continuously during the period of conversion from war to peace, as the war ended and we entered the period of peace, the same need continued to exist, though in different forms and with the same object, namely, to spread abroad knowledge and information about. Canada as the basis of international understanding and, we hope, trade and security. But, further, we found that we were getting from countries like Brazil orders which were traceable not only to the fact that we had the goods but also to the fact that there was an understanding of Canada built up in Brazil. That, as I say, was traceable, in part, to Brazil's information about Canada. There was that understanding and confidence built up in that way. speechtext:
I wish to make some general observations about the film board before we proceed with this vote. First of all, I should like to say a word on the subject of economy, taking my text from what the Minister of Finance said last night when he spoke about the necessity of equating revenue and expenditures at a time when we have high employment and high national income. The minister spoke to us about taking our responsibilities in this matter seriously. I did not like very much that part of his speech where he said that the suggestions from this side of the house for economy had been pathetic, that there was merely a tiny suggestion here and a tiny suggestion there. With all due respect to the minister, I would point out that I made suggestions of economy which totalled $60,000,000. If the minister thinks that is tiny and pathetic I want t'o tell him that in the constituency of Muskoka-Ontario $60,000,000 is a lot of money.
I wanted to make one or two general observations about the film board. At the outset I want to be specific in saying that I believe the film board has done useful work and can continue to do useful work, but I want to say also that I think there is a danger that new and interesting inventions may sometimes get the bit in their teeth and run away with themselves and with us and our money in a way that we should be careful about.
I have in my hand a finely got up pamphlet called "Image". This was published by the film board and is an attractive piece of advertising for the work of the board. It is done on quite nice paper which I think most of us would find it difficult to get. It begins with a most interesting letter from a gentleman well known to us, Mr. John Grierson. I regret to say that in this letter he makes some reference to the Scotch race which I

Supply-Film Board
greatly deprecate and which I am sure the Minister of Veterans Affairs will deprecate. Mr. Grieraon must be a renegade Scot, because he takes a loose view with regard to money. Mr. Grierson quotes a remark made by Mr. Winston Churchill at the end of the first war as follows:
One remembers Mr. Churchill's comment about armistice day 1918:	"A new set of conditions
began to rule from eleven o'clock onwards. The money cost, which had never been a factor capable of limiting the supply to the armies, asserted a claim to priority the moment the fighting stopped."
That was a quotation from Mr. Churchill, and Mr. Grierson added, "the results we all know". Then Mr. Grierson comes to that part to which I object, and he refers to the Scotch in the following words:
We may expect the worthies, particularly my fellow worthies of Scottish lineage, to recall their stern and frugal upbringing and dedicate themselves, with moral unction, to starving to death.
He apparently regards anything that is not spending wildly without limit as starving to death. He goes on to refer to the atomic age when apparently everything will be wonderful. In this interesting pamphlet certain references are made to the expansion of the board and I should like to refer briefly to these. I am not objecting to the expansion of the board, I am only saying that at a time when we are so heavily taxed, when we are faced with such deficits, we should count our pennies.
I want to say a little about the organization of the board, and in this connection I should like to quote from a page entitled, "Report from Washington". We have here an organization which I think is in danger of taking the bit in its teeth and running away with itself and with us. I feel we should take stock of it and make sure it is doing what we want it to do, in the way we want it to do it and in the way that other departments are doing. I quote:
The national film board of Canada has been an active agent in the Washington film scene now for well over two years.
It then goes on to refer to the setting up of the Washington office, and reference is made in the following words to one of the transactions which have taken place:
During the past year more than 400 American films produced by or for the United States have gone to Canada for deposit in the film board's preview film library.	.
I skip again and read from the bottom of
the paragraph*:
By reason of their larger share in the war information budgets the O.W.I., treasury, army and navy have taken the lead in the mass distribution of Canadian films, primarily orientation and morale subjects such as "Fortress Japan," "New Soldiers are Tough," and "The Peace Builders."
I do not know why these war-time films should go on now, but apparently they still like them in the United States.
I should like to read briefly from the public accounts for the year ended March 31, 1945, and I do this in order to bring to the attention of the committee a report of the auditor general in which, speaking of the national film board, he says:
The board does not invariably follow practices which regulate departments of government. In the course of audit it was observed that purchases of articles, costing $627.95, had been made from public employees without first obtaining the customary concurrence of treasury board.
After citing one or two other things, the report states:
Order in council P.C. 107/5547 of July 19 1944, authorizes the board to pay a newsreel film editor a monthly living allowance of $40 while on an assignment in New York. Effect has not been given to this plan. Instead, in the period from August 1 to March 31 he was paid living expenses on the basis of a detailed accounting. Hotel and meal charges were $1,981.45. When converted into Canadian dollars, these payments average $275 monthly.
I am not suggesting that $40 a month is sufficient for a gentleman who has to live in New York, and I do not know why that amount was put in the order in council, but I am suggesting that it would have been desirable if it was to be changed that the change be made by the authorities who authorized the original amount. It should not have been left to the film board itself to multiply by about six what apparently the order in Council thought was sufficient for the purpose.
In making these preliminary observations and before coming to the details of the accounts, I just wish to emphasize what I said at the outset, that we should regard this new invention, this interesting tool, as something we ought to make use of, but I feel that there is a danger with these new inventions that they take charge of us and acquire a privileged position and are not subject to the same limitations as the less romantic and exciting and artistic government departments. I think we are entitled to look at the figures in the light of that, and also to ask the minister to give us a considerable amount of information as to the relationship of the board to the trade. Therefore I am proposing to ask a considerable number of questions.
I think the committee has already been told members of the board and the details of

their appointment, the name of the film commissioner and the date of his appointment. I would ask now, what is the relation between the board and the various departments of the government? On what basis are films produced for or on behalf of the various departments of government? On what basis are they paid for?

With regard to the quotation made by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario from the piece by Mr. John Grierson in "Image", Mr. John Grierson, as he knows, as well as other hon. members, is about as Scotch a Scotsman as you can find anywhere on the face of the earth.

With regard to the item in public accounts,
I should tell the hon. member that the item was dealt with in a way which was authorized by the treasury board itself, and it was cleared up during the accounting period in question now to the board's satisfaction. The discrepancy between the living allowance authorized and the actual allowance required was taken care of by a submission to treasury board, which thereupon approved the living allowance which was actually needed, and which was established. speechtext: That is the difficulty with these accounts; they are so far behind.

subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext:
Yes, There is no other way in which the public accounts can be dealt with. They have to be dealt with in arrears because of the size of the operations of government.
The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario asked what relation was there between the board and the departments of government which ordered films. The board produces films for other government departments, and in the course of its work it produces a very

large quantity of films for other government departments. It is done in this way. If, for example, the army wants to have a film of, let us say, "Exercise Muskox", the responsible officers in the army get in touch with the officers of the film board and say: We want to get a film of "Exercise Muskox" for use in instruction. Or they may say: We want a film made for some other purpose. The film board then arranges to send with the expedition a film crew, the composition of which is worked out with the army, and the required quantity of moving and still pictures are taken, and then are subsequently edited into the kind of films that the army wants. I mention "Exercise Muskox" as a typical example. As a consequence of that, the army will very shortly have a film which will run for about an hour and be suitable for their purposes. In addition, as a by-product the national film board itself will produce a film this month in the "Canada Carries On" series, which will be shown through the commercial theatres of Canada on all commercial circuits and which will give a good picture of the kind of country and the kind of operation in which "Exercise Muskox" was engaged.

subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: When that film is shown on the commercial circuits will the commercial circuits be paying commercial prices for it, and will the government of Canada make a profit or loss on the showing of that film?

speechtext:
It will be shown at
ordinary commercial rates, but the market for short subjects in Canada is such that ordinarily you cannot get a price for shorts produced in Canada which would enable the film to be produced at a profit.

subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: There was another side to my question. Are the films paid for by the departments which order them, and, if so, on what basis?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare

speechtext: They are paid for by the departments which order them on the basis of the cost of production. The film board itself has a cost accounting system, which enables the cost of each film to be allocated to that film; and then a certain percentage is added for overhead. The total amount is charged to the department, which then makes the payment, covering the actual cost of that film.

The estimates for the film board for this year are found in three items in these estimates, votes 244, 245 and 246, in a total of $1,106,465, and three items, votes 581, 582 and 583 in the demobilization and reconversion estimates for a total of $1,030,683. The corresponding figures for the ordinary estimates for the previous year, 1945-46, will be found in vote 230, for $810,965, and the war appropriation is to be found at page 556 of Hansard, September 28, 1945, of $1,780,000, as well as vote 537 in the supplementary estimates for $335,000, making a total of $2,925,965. This amount includes a revolving fund of $500,000. Apart from the revolving fund, the amount sought for this year represents a reduction of $288,817, or twelve per cent, from the amount sought last year. The amount also that the board anticipates to obtain from other government departments will be substantially reduced, because a large sum was provided for war activities of the armed forces, the national war finance committee and other government activities which related particularly to the war.
The national film board filed its annual report covering the period ended March 31, 1945, in October, 1945. The annual report for the year ended 31st March, 1946, will be filed as soon as possible.
During the year, film board officials, in consultation with the auditor general and the comptroller of the treasury, have made a 63260-230i
number of improvements in the system of accounting which have been designed to reconcile the situation brought about through the film board being in some respects analagous to a commercial undertaking and at the same time an agency of the government. To carry out still further the recommendations of the auditor general, the form in which the estimates are presented has been changed to provide funds for general and technical administration. These funds were formerly secured by assessing an overhead charge against each production.
During the year under review, that is 194546, the film board has carried on its activities in many fields. Altogether a total of 310 film subjects have been produced. speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: There are quite a number devoted to that purpose, and I will give the hon. member full information about them as I come to it in my notes.

subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: I think it would be valuable to have the names of these films put on record.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: COORDINATION OF AND ASSISTANCE TO GOVERNMENT INFORMATION SERVICE
speechtext: I shall be glad to do that. I warn hon. members that it will be lengthy; it will take up several pages of Hansard, but if there is unanimous consent, and at the request of the committee, I shall be glad to do it. As I say, it will occupy several pages.
